summary: Defines an extension of the TCP Selective Acknowledgement option, letting a receiver report duplicate segments it has received. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a friend gets parts of a message twice, they can tell you which parts, so you know what happened to your mail.

questions: how does tcp report duplicate segments
what is the tcp sack option kind
how to detect unnecessary retransmission in tcp
subtitle: How a TCP receiver can use the SACK option to tell the sender which data arrived more than once.

tldr.problem: RFC 2018 defined the SACK option for out-of-order data but said nothing about what to report when a duplicate segment arrives, so a TCP sender could not tell why data showed up twice.
tldr.mechanism: When a duplicate arrives, the receiver puts a D-SACK block describing the duplicated sequence numbers first in the SACK option, followed by the usual SACK blocks.
tldr.outcome: The sender can detect replication in the network, a false retransmit caused by reordering, a timeout caused by lost ACKs, and an early retransmission timeout. The RFC specifies the detection, not what the sender should then do.

today: RFC 2883 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds directly on RFC 2018.

sections.title: The Problem With Duplicates
sections.content:
The SACK option from RFC 2018 lets a TCP receiver acknowledge non-contiguous blocks of data that the cumulative acknowledgement field does not cover. What RFC 2018 does not specify is the use of the SACK option when a duplicate segment is received.

This note fills that gap. It uses the term D-SACK (duplicate-SACK) for a SACK block that reports a duplicate segment. It changes nothing about how the cumulative acknowledgement field is used, or about when the receiver decides to send an acknowledgement. It only concerns the contents of the SACK option once an acknowledgement is being sent.
sections.eli5: The old rules said how to report pieces that arrive out of order, but not what to say when the same piece arrives twice. This document adds that rule.

sections.title: The SACK Option Before D-SACK
sections.content:
A SACK option is carried in the TCP header with Kind=5 and a length, followed by pairs of 32-bit edges. Each block gives a left edge, the first sequence number of the block, and a right edge, the sequence number immediately following the last sequence number of the block.

RFC 2018 already says the first SACK block MUST specify the contiguous block of data containing the segment that triggered the ACK, unless that segment advanced the Acknowledgment Number field. It also says SACK options SHOULD be included in all ACKs that do not acknowledge the highest sequence number in the receiver's queue. That leaves a gap: when a duplicate arrives and the cumulative acknowledgement already covers all queued data, no rule says what the SACK option should contain.
sections.eli5: A SACK block is like saying 'I have pages 5 to 9'. The first block was already supposed to describe the page that just arrived.

sections.title: Reporting a Duplicate Segment
sections.content:
When D-SACK is used, the first block of the SACK option is a D-SACK block giving the sequence numbers of the duplicate segment that triggered the acknowledgement. If that segment is part of a larger block of non-contiguous data in the receiver's queue, the second SACK block specifies that larger block. Any further blocks report other non-contiguous data, as in RFC 2018.

  • A D-SACK block reports only a duplicate contiguous sequence received in the most recent packet.
  • Each duplicate sequence is reported in at most one D-SACK block. Two identical D-SACK blocks in later packets mean two duplicate segments arrived.
  • The left edge is the first sequence number of the duplicate, and the right edge is the sequence number immediately following its last.

Because each duplicate is reported only once, the information is lost if that ACK is dropped. For a packet that is only partly duplicate, for example after the sender's segment size grows when the path MTU increases mid-session, the first D-SACK block reports the first duplicate sub-segment. Only that first one is reported.
sections.eli5: The receiver puts the 'I got this twice' note first, so the sender cannot miss it. Each repeat is announced once, so if that one note gets lost, the news is lost too.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives six examples. In each, the receiver has first received eight segments of 500 bytes and sent a cumulative acknowledgement of 4000, assuming the first sequence number is zero.

In the first, several ACKs are lost, so the sender retransmits 3000-3499. The receiver gets a duplicate and replies with cumulative ACK 4000 and first block SACK=3000-3500. In the second, an out-of-order segment 4500-4999 had already produced SACK=4500-5000, and the duplicate then yields SACK=3000-3500, 4500-5000. In the third, a duplicate of an out-of-order segment gives SACK=5000-5500, 4500-5500: the D-SACK block first, then the larger block it belongs to.

Examples four to six cover partial duplicates, where a larger retransmitted packet contains a mix of old and new data, and show that only the first duplicate sub-segment is reported.
sections.eli5: In every example the pattern is the same: the repeated piece is named first, and then the receiver lists everything else it is holding.

sections.title: Compatibility and PAWS
sections.content:
D-SACK needs no separate negotiation once SACK has been negotiated. If the sender does not understand the extension, it simply discards the D-SACK block and processes the other SACK blocks as normal. The RFC states that it believes use by only one end node will not introduce problems.

The extension also fits with Protection Against Wrapped Sequence Numbers (PAWS) from RFC 1323. PAWS still requires an ACK to be sent for a segment it drops, so the D-SACK block can be included regardless of what PAWS decides. A reported duplicate might have come from a prior cycle through the sequence number space; the authors do not expect this to be a significant problem for senders.
sections.eli5: If the sender has never heard of D-SACK, it just ignores the extra note. Nothing breaks.

sections.title: What the Sender Can Detect
sections.content:
To check that the first block really reports duplicate data, the sender compares it with the cumulative ACK carried in the same packet. If the block lies below that ACK, the data was received more than once. An implementation MUST NOT compare it to the state variable snd.una, because that can give the wrong answer if ACKs are reordered. If the block lies above the cumulative ACK, the sender compares it with the second block to see if it is duplicate data above the ACK.

The RFC walks through four situations a sender following RFC 2581 might see: replication by the network, a false retransmit caused by packets reordered by more than 3 packets, a retransmit timeout caused by loss of an entire window of ACKs, and an early retransmission timeout when the RTO is too short. In each, D-SACK gives the sender positive knowledge it would otherwise lack.

The document does not specify what a sender should do in response. It lists research issues, such as adjusting the duplicate acknowledgment threshold, adjusting RTO parameters, or undoing a congestion window reduction, and notes that any such scheme must consider that the receiver might be lying.
sections.eli5: The sender can now tell apart 'my message was lost', 'my message was just slow' and 'only the reply was lost'. What to do about it is left for later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is one sentence: this document neither strengthens nor weakens TCP's current security properties. Elsewhere it does warn that a sender cannot necessarily trust the receiver to report accurately.
sections.eli5: It does not make TCP safer or less safe, but a sender should remember the receiver might fib.
